You initially misidentify the fault as the motor. What do you do after the first wrong diagnosis?", "You remember a workshop rule from earlier today: never run the old press twice in the same session. What do you do?", "Your phone notes contain three repair observations: a loose gear clicked twice, the cabinet vibrated near the compressor, and a bolt was tested six times. Only the first note is clearly connected to today’s job. What do you do with the rest?", "A colleague tells you, “Don’t touch the hot bearing,” but forgets the rest of the sentence. You want to save it and test it. What do you do?", "A colleague asks you to certify that a machine is safe after a near-miss. You can see the vibration and feel the heat, but the test data looks clean. What do you say?", "You are asked to make a quiet display motor spin smoothly and predictably, but the motor’s best behavior appears when its bearing is slightly loose. What do you do?", "A friend says, “I’m not touching that machine until it stops making that awful noise.” How do you respond?", "During a workshop demonstration, a visitor asks why you keep a visibly damaged gear beside a working machine. What do you tell them?", "You are making coffee in the workshop while the ultrasonic cleaner is running. What do you notice before taking the first sip?", "A desk fan wobbles across the table, but it is not important. What do you do?", "A sandwich toaster drops one corner of the bread into a narrow slot. How do you deal with it?", "A motor control board has been running all afternoon in the workshop, and a faint burnt-plastic smell is drifting from beneath its cover. What do you do first?", "You are holding a screwdriver against a cabinet while the pump starts. A faint vibration travels through the handle and into your palm. What is your immediate response?", "A freshly welded steel bracket is cooling beside the bench. You need to know whether it is still hot enough to deform when touched. What do you do?", "A small conveyor has one roller that squeaks under load but runs perfectly when empty. You have time for one adjustment before the demonstration. What do you choose?", "A workshop display motor has a faint catch in its bearing, but removing the bearing would make the display quieter and more predictable. The original bearing is still reversible. What do you do?", "You find a bolt seated loosely in a bracket. Tightening it would make the bracket rigid, but leaving it slightly loose may reveal how the load transfers. Which do you choose?", "After changing a motor's direction switch, it runs once, stops, and will not restart on the same setting. What do you do after the failed attempt?", "Your first attempt to free a seized gearbox shears three teeth from the drive gear. The gearbox is still locked, but the teeth are intact enough to examine. What do you do?", "A demonstration rig suddenly locks during a public run. The motor is fine, but the coupling is hot and one fastener is missing. What do you do next?", "You remember a workshop rule from yesterday: never run the blue pump twice in one session. You cannot remember the reason, and the pump is idling beside you. What do you do?", "Your phone notes contain three observations from earlier jobs: a loose gear clicked twice, the cabinet vibrated near the compressor, and a bolt was tested six times. Only the first note clearly belongs to today's repair. What do you do with the other two?", "You remember applying a specific torque to a pump housing this morning, but you cannot recall whether that was the correct torque or just the one that stopped the wobble. What do you do before adjusting it again?", "An office chair in the workshop has developed a faint squeak whenever you lean back. What do you do?", "A vending machine rejects your coin without dropping it into the tray. What do you do?", "Your phone charging cable fits only if you hold it at a particular angle, but the phone still charges. What do you do?", "A colleague asks, “Why does that motor sound better now that you loosened the mount?” How do you answer?", "A visitor says, “A good machine should be silent and smooth. Why are you letting that one wobble?” What do you tell them?", "A rare original gear spins beautifully, but its looseness makes the display machine catch and shudder. You can preserve the gear untouched or keep it installed for one more test. What do you do?", "A test motor runs fastest with the housing slightly loose, but that same looseness creates heat near the insulation. You have one short test window. What do you do?", "You are asked to build a demonstration that is both perfectly consistent and deliberately unpredictable. The constraints seem to lock each other. What do you do?", "A brake caliper in the workshop is still ticking as it cools. What do you do the moment you notice?", "A sealed motor housing gives off a sharp, acrid smell while the current is cut. What is your first bodily response?", "A plastic casing begins ticking against its mounting plate during a brief test. What do you do as the first tick reaches your hand?", "A bench grinder has a slightly worn pulley that produces a characteristic flutter at one speed. You need a smooth demonstration, but the worn pulley is also the part that reveals the grinder’s behavior. Which do you choose?", "A small display gearbox can run silently with its cover tightened, or turn more freely if the cover is backed off by half a turn. You are asked to make the mechanism move visibly. What do you do?", "A salvaged motor runs well only when its bearing is slightly loose. You need it for a brief public test, and the loose fit is reversible. What do you choose?", "You repeat the same adjustment on a ratcheting mechanism until it stops advancing, although the same instruction worked twice before. What do you do next?", "Your first attempt to diagnose a clicking gearbox blames the motor. The motor passes every test, but the gearbox still clicks and warms. What do you do after the wrong diagnosis?", "A stripped gear breaks loose during your test and jams the shaft. You wanted to observe its behavior, not sacrifice it. What do you recover?", "You remember that a small brass gear on the bench clicked once per turn yesterday, but you cannot remember which machine it came from. It is loose in your palm now. What do you do?", "A note says only: “Blue housing—three turns, then wait.” You remember testing a bolt this way last week, but not whether it tightened or loosened. What do you do before touching it again?", "You remember that yesterday’s repaired pump ran briefly, then warmed near the coupling. Today the coupling feels warm almost immediately. What do you do with that fading recollection?", "You want to keep watching a nearly smooth spindle, but the same test cycle keeps producing the same catch and beginning to warm the bearing. You have one adjustment left. What do you do?", "A rare original coupling fits beautifully but makes the test rig shudder. You want to preserve it, yet you also want the demonstration to run cleanly. What do you choose?", "You could make the display more dramatic by introducing a controlled misalignment, but the instructions demand a perfectly repeatable run. What do you do?", "A colleague says, “Why loosen a working mount just to watch it shake?” How do you answer?", "A visitor watches you label a badly chipped gear and asks, “Why keep that broken thing instead of throwing it away?” How do you respond?", "A paper cup on your workshop bench develops a small dent while you are reaching past it. What do you do?", "Your desk chair has developed a faint wobble while you are typing at the workshop computer. What do you do?", "A plastic tray on the counter keeps sliding a few millimeters whenever you pull it toward you. What do you do?"]
